items.prompt: In the NP “those copper lanterns”, which word is the noun head?

options.rationale: The phrase denotes lanterns; this noun heads the NP.
This determiner does not name the kind of thing.
This pre-head modifier is not the head of this NP.

items.rationale: Lanterns is the noun head; do not confuse the whole NP with its head.

items.prompt: Which complete group can be replaced by “they” in “The curious otters vanished”?

options.rationale: The pronoun replaces the complete subject NP.
The adjective alone is not the subject NP.
This crosses the subject–predicate boundary.

items.rationale: They vanished preserves the predicate and replaces the whole NP.

items.prompt: In “Leena smiled”, what is the phrasal category of “Leena”?

options.rationale: A name can form a one-word noun phrase.
Smiled, not Leena, forms the predicate VP.
Subject names a function, not a category.

items.rationale: A phrase need not contain several words; NP and subject answer different questions.

items.prompt: Compare “a wooden bridge” and “several wooden bridges”. Which pair shows the noun's singular/plural contrast?

options.rationale: These are singular and plural forms of the noun.
These are different words, not noun number forms.
The modifier has not changed number.

items.rationale: The count noun head changes from bridge to bridges.

items.prompt: In “The gardener collected seeds”, does the category NP determine whether a phrase is subject or object?

options.text: No: both “the gardener” and “seeds” are NPs with different functions.
options.rationale: Category and grammatical function are distinct.

options.text: Yes: every NP is a subject.
options.rationale: Seeds is an object NP here.

options.text: Yes: every NP is an object.
options.rationale: The gardener is the subject NP here.

items.rationale: The same phrasal category can serve different grammatical functions.

items.prompt: Which form of “write” occurs after perfect “has” in “Nadia has written a note”?

options.rationale: Perfect have selects a past-participial complement.
The preterite form is wrote.
The plain form is write.

items.rationale: Written is the past participle, distinct from preterite wrote.

items.prompt: In “The kestrel flew away”, which inflectional form is “flew”?

options.rationale: Flew is the preterite form of fly.
The past participle is flown.
The gerund-participle is flying.

items.rationale: Flew, flown and flying are distinct inflectional forms.

items.prompt: Which form appears after “may” in “The lock may freeze tonight”?

options.rationale: Modal may selects the plain form freeze.
That form is freezes, which is not selected after may.
The preterite is froze.

items.rationale: Freeze here is a plain form selected by a modal auxiliary.

items.prompt: What is the form of “swimming” in “The seals are swimming”?

options.rationale: Cambridge uses this form name for the verb's -ing form.
The past participle is swum.
Swimming is not the plain present swim.

items.rationale: The progressive uses be with a gerund-participial complement.

items.prompt: Compare “We cut the ribbon yesterday” and “We have cut the ribbon”. Must identical spelling mean identical inflectional form?

options.text: No: the first is preterite, the second past participle.
options.rationale: Different forms can share their spelling and pronunciation.
Perfect have selects a past participle.

options.text: Yes: both are necessarily plain forms.
options.rationale: The contexts distinguish the relevant forms.

items.rationale: Form identity cannot be inferred from spelling alone; these forms are syncretic.
